lesson.title: Building a New World Order: The Founding of the United Nations
lesson.summary: In 1945 the Allied powers created the United Nations to prevent future world wars through collective security and diplomacy, learning from the failure of the League of Nations after World War I.
lesson.body:
Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, presented to Congress in January 1918, had called for a "general association of nations" to preserve peace after World War I. That vision became the League of Nations, but the United States Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and 1920, largely because senators led by Henry Cabot Lodge feared that joining the League, especially its Article X, would drag the United States into future wars without a full congressional vote. Without American participation, the League proved too weak to stop aggression by Japan, Italy, and Germany in the 1930s, and by 1939 the world was at war again.

Franklin Roosevelt was determined not to repeat that mistake. On January 1, 1942, twenty six nations fighting the Axis powers signed the Declaration by United Nations, the first official use of the name Roosevelt had chosen. Through the rest of the war, American, British, and Soviet diplomats worked out the details of a new international organization, most importantly at the Dumbarton Oaks Conference held in Washington DC in the fall of 1944. There the major Allied powers agreed on the basic structure: a General Assembly where every member nation would have a voice, and a Security Council with real enforcement power.

The Yalta Conference in February 1945 settled one of the thorniest remaining questions. Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin agreed that five countries, the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, France, and China, would sit as permanent members of the Security Council with veto power over major decisions. Stalin had insisted on the veto because he did not trust the Soviet Union to get a fair hearing from a Western dominated Assembly, and Roosevelt accepted it as the price of Soviet participation. This compromise gave the UN more teeth than the League of Nations ever had, but it also meant the organization could be paralyzed whenever the great powers disagreed with each other, a problem that became obvious almost as soon as the Cold War began.

Roosevelt died on April 12, 1945, just weeks before delegates from fifty nations gathered in San Francisco to write the UN Charter. The San Francisco Conference ran from April 25 to June 26, 1945, and President Truman, now in charge, pushed hard to see Roosevelt's vision through. The Charter was signed on June 26, and the United Nations officially came into existence on October 24, 1945, once enough countries, including all five permanent Security Council members, had ratified it. Unlike after World War I, the United States Senate approved American membership without a fight, a sign of how thoroughly the experience of two world wars had changed American attitudes toward international engagement.
